title: ICE paid $495.6 million for an empty Minnesota prison. The state had been offered it for $75 million.
dek: CoreCivic's shuttered Appleton facility is assessed at $14.75 million. The sale closed the day it was signed, the company bought back $500 million of its own stock six days later, and the Treasury secretary, in Minnesota to announce a fraud crackdown, called the question a waste of time.
body:
On August 4, the United States government, acting through the Department of Homeland Security, bought a prison in Appleton, Minnesota, that had stood empty for sixteen years. The seller, the private prison company CoreCivic, reported the price in a securities filing the next day: about $495.6 million for the 1,600-bed Prairie Correctional Facility and some related assets [5]. The purchase agreement was signed and the sale closed on the same day [5].

Fifteen months earlier, in May 2025, CoreCivic had offered the same building to the State of Minnesota for $75 million, an offer the state's Department of Corrections confirmed this week after KARE 11, the NBC affiliate in Minneapolis, reported it [1][2]. Swift County, which collects the property taxes, put the facility's total market value for 2026 at $14.75 million [2]. The federal government paid about $420 million more than the state was asked to pay, more than six times the price [3][11].

The gap has drawn the Minnesota attorney general's call for a congressional investigation, a U.S. senator's public questions and a corrections commissioner who says he cannot explain it [2][3]. On Friday it followed the Treasury secretary to St. Cloud, where he had come to announce a federal crackdown on Minnesota fraud and said a question about the prison was a waste of time [10][12]. What follows is what is known about the building, the two prices and the money behind them. The Watch's analysis of the wider record, [the fraud hunters' ledger](https://bboldt86.github.io/lanscape-navigator/news/#/a/2026-10-31-minnesota-fraud-hunters-ledger-two-dead-citizens-420-million-prison), and tonight's Late Night piece, [the Main Story](https://bboldt86.github.io/lanscape-navigator/news/#/ln/2026-10-31-the-main-story-fraud-task-force-420-million-prison), start from here.

## A prison built on spec

The city of Appleton, a small town in west-central Minnesota, built the prison itself and opened it in 1992, before it had anyone to put in it; its first inmates came from Puerto Rico the next year [14]. The company then known as Corrections Corporation of America bought it in 1997, expanded it twice and filled it with prisoners from Colorado, Idaho, Wisconsin, Hawaii, Washington and Minnesota, among other states [14]. It closed in 2010 after Minnesota added beds of its own at Faribault and Moose Lake and no longer needed the space [14].

For most of the years since, the building has been a political football in St. Paul. Republican legislators pushed the state to buy or lease it in 2017, promising hundreds of local jobs; many prison guards came to the hearing to oppose it, and the state kept sending its overflow to county jails instead [15]. A 2023 House bill would have barred the Department of Corrections from housing prisoners in privately owned prisons at all, with supporters noting that Appleton is far from a major hospital and from the Twin Cities, where most inmates' families live [14].

That distance is also why the state turned down CoreCivic's offer last year. According to KARE 11's reporting, as summarized by The Independent, the $75 million price included upgrades to the facility, but officials balked at staffing a site nearly three hours from Minneapolis-St. Paul and at the cost of housing the roughly 500 employees it would need [3]. ICE did not share those concerns [3].

## What the federal government bought

By the summer of 2025 CoreCivic was pursuing an ICE contract for the building, and an ICE planning document from that July listed it among the sites for a national expansion of detention [14]. A proposed DHS contract that MPR News reported earlier this year said the facility was needed to meet the administration's "interior enforcement and border compression goals" and would serve ICE's St. Paul field office [4].

CoreCivic announced on August 5 that it had sold Prairie, along with its 1,033-bed Midwest Regional Reception Center in Leavenworth, Kansas, to the government for a combined $734 million; Leavenworth went for about $238.4 million [5]. The company said it expected to clear about $522.5 million from the two sales after taxes of about $182.2 million and transaction costs [5]. The month before, it had sold two California detention centers to DHS, Otay Mesa in San Diego County and the newly opened California City facility, for $739.2 million and $732.6 million [7]. Four prisons, one summer, about $2.2 billion [3].

Selling the building did not mean leaving it. CoreCivic keeps running Prairie under a five-year management contract that started August 11 and runs to August 2031, and it told investors it expects about $75 million a year in revenue from the site, a fixed monthly payment plus a daily rate for each detainee [4]. ICE can end the contract for convenience or if Congress does not appropriate the money [4]. The company said it had opened preliminary talks with ICE about selling it more facilities [5]. Detainees were expected this fall, with the facility full by mid-2027; residents have organized a weekly protest outside it [4].

The same day the Prairie and Leavenworth agreements were signed, CoreCivic's board expanded the company's stock buyback authority to $755.8 million [6]. Six days later the company agreed to spend $500 million of cash on hand buying back its own shares [6].

## How the price was set

CoreCivic has said the government, not the company, set the number. A spokesperson told KARE 11 that independent appraisers used a cost-based method and that "the federal government ultimately determined the sale price following its assessment process" [2][3]. In the California sales the company described the same approach: an appraisal built on replacement cost, depreciation and land value, which it said the government had reviewed for compliance with federal standards [7].

A cost-based appraisal asks what it would take to build the thing again, not what anyone would pay for it. By that measure a 1,600-bed prison can be worth hundreds of millions even if the only buyer in fifteen years was willing to pay $75 million and the county assessor says $14.75 million. By the arithmetic of the two offers, the state was asked for about $47,000 a bed and the federal government paid about $310,000 a bed, for a building that still needs work before it can hold anyone [2][5][12].

Minnesota's corrections commissioner, Paul Schnell, who received the $75 million offer, told KARE 11 the federal price was unexplainable and that he was stunned when he saw it, given what his department had been offered a little over a year before [13]. He said he still could not figure it out [12].

The same pattern shows up in the federal government's other purchases. Bring Me The News noted that the Otay Mesa center, bought for $739 million, carried an assessed value of $160 million, and that DHS reportedly paid at least double the estimated value for eleven warehouses it planned to convert into detention centers early this year, some at up to ten times their estimated worth [2].

## Where the money comes from

The purchases are possible because of the budget law enacted in July 2025, which gave ICE $45 billion through fiscal 2029 to expand detention, against about $3.8 billion in ordinary appropriations for detention facilities in fiscal 2025 [9]. ICE's average daily detained population rose 71 percent in that time, from about 39,300 people on January 20, 2025, to nearly 67,200 on July 30, 2026 [9].

The Government Accountability Office looked at how the money is being spent and, on September 24, titled its report "Urgent Planning Needed to Avoid Further Waste of Taxpayer Dollars" [8]. It found that ICE had pursued six new detention initiatives without the analysis and planning they required and had no comprehensive strategic plan for the expansion [8]. The eleven warehouses cost about $1.07 billion; by June ICE was trying to sell seven of them, bought for $707 million, and had spent more than $20 million on zoning, security and utilities it will never get back [8][9]. The GAO said ICE had not weighed high-cost facilities against cheaper options in its existing portfolio and lacked information about the long-term affordability of what it was buying [8][9]. DHS agreed to write a plan. ICE said it would be done by August 31, 2027 [8].

CoreCivic, for its part, gave $500,000 to the Trump-Vance inaugural committee and reported spending $1.77 million lobbying on the budget bill, according to Bring Me The News [2]. After the second inauguration the company's chief executive told investors it was anticipating significant growth opportunities [13].

## The reaction, and the non-answer

Attorney General Keith Ellison asked the House and Senate Homeland Security committees and the House Oversight Committee to investigate, describing a $420 million overpayment and calling the deal a scam on taxpayers [2][3]. Senator Tina Smith posted that ICE evidently had enough money to spend nearly $500 million on a prison first offered for $75 million [2]. KARE 11 described the sale as the most expensive property purchase in Minnesota's history [13]. Racket, the Minneapolis news site, pointed out that the premium alone is larger than the estimated loss in Feeding Our Future, the pandemic meals fraud that the administration cites as the emblem of Minnesota's problems [13][11].

On Friday morning the question reached the administration directly. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel and the Medicare and Medicaid administrator Mehmet Oz were in St. Cloud, under a banner for the vice president's fraud task force, to announce the arrests of four Medicaid providers accused of defrauding the program of about $41 million [10][11]. Vice President JD Vance had canceled late the night before [11]. Bessent said fraud was all over the state and blamed Governor Tim Walz's administration for turning a blind eye to it [11].

KARE 11's Lou Raguse asked him to explain the $420 million overpayment in Appleton. Bessent said he did not know anything about it, that the task force was there to prosecute criminal fraud, and that any question meant to deflect from that "is a waste of our time" [10][12]. DHS and ICE had not answered the outlets that asked them about the price [2][3].

## What to watch

- **Whether Congress takes it up.** Ellison has asked three committees, all Republican-led, to investigate [2]. Of Minnesota's delegation, Senator Smith has spoken up publicly [2].
- **An appraisal, if there is one.** CoreCivic says the government assessed the property; neither the company nor DHS has released the appraisal or the method behind the $495.6 million figure [2][3][7].
- **The first detainees.** The facility was due to start taking people this fall under a contract that pays CoreCivic by the day as well as by the month [4]. The GAO's warning was about facilities ICE bought and could not use; a full Appleton would at least settle that question [8].
- **The next sale.** CoreCivic has told investors it is talking with ICE about more [5]. The budget law's $45 billion runs through 2029 [9].
